question: Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stated in the context of the strategic dialogue on the future of the automotive industry: ‘We need European car supply chains to be more robust and more resilient, especially when it comes to batteries […]. We will explore direct support for EU battery producers. We will gradually introduce European content requirements for battery cells and components’.
Given the significant cost gap with China and increasingly with the United States, market uncertainties and the need for transitional production support: 1.

Will the mentioned forms of direct production support for EU battery producers – aimed at bridging this competitiveness gap, especially in the critical 5 to 6-year scaling phase – include output-based support and will it be provided under the new multiannual financial framework for the 2028-2034 period or under the current multiannual financial framework?

What timeline and content requirements does the Commission envisage for the battery sector and how will these measures be coordinated with demand-side policies to ensure the long-term market certainty necessary for gigafactory investments and to mitigate further dependence on imported batteries?

The Commission recommended and adopted tariffs on electric vehicles from China. Is it also considering tariffs on batteries to counter the artificially low prices driven by production overcapacity in China?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.4.2026) The Commission has announced up to EUR 3 billion of the Innovation Fund for Electric Vehicle (EV) battery manufacturing, starting with a call for proposals of EUR 1 billion concluded in 2025. A partnership between the Commission and the European Investment Bank has added a EUR 200 million top-up to InvestEU1 to support innovative EU battery manufacturing projects.

The remaining amount will be used to provide support through the Battery Booster package2. For the next Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-2034, a Competitiveness Fund3 is proposed, which integrates InvestEU and allows support for industrial manufacturing ramp-up.

The Commission has proposed the inclusion of EU content requirements, in line with the EU’s international legal commitments, under the Industrial Accelerator Act proposal, adopted on 4 March 20264. These requirements have been carefully calibrated to assess their impact and ensure that European industry remains competitive, resilient and aligned with Europe’s broader industrial and climate goals.

These will complement the initiatives outlined in the Battery booster strategy5, which includes measures for securing raw materials, scaling production, ensuring offtake and maintaining a level playing field.

The Commission recalls that the adoption of duties on imports of Battery EVs from China was the result of an investigation into the injurious effects of such imports, a process and decision that were governed by Regulation (EU) 2016/10376. There is no such investigation ongoing on imports of batteries. The Commission continues to monitor closely the situation of the EV supply chains.
